content: Iron-deficiency anemia is a prevalent condition during childhood, particularly in regions where malaria is endemic. There has been concern that iron supplementation might increase the risk of malaria in such areas. This study aimed to assess the effects and safety of oral iron supplementation, with or without folic acid, in children living in regions with high or continuous malaria transmission. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and LILACS, up to February 2015. They also reviewed trial registries, contacted primary investigators for unpublished data, and examined references from relevant studies and meta-analyses. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in hyperendemic or holoendemic malaria regions, involving children under 18 years of age. Trials were included if they compared oral iron (alone or with folic acid or antimalarial treatment) to placebo or no treatment, provided at least 80% of the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for iron, and ensured equal administration of other micronutrients to both groups. The primary outcomes assessed were clinical malaria, severe malaria, and all-cause mortality. The researchers evaluated the risk of bias using a domain-based approach and assessed the quality of evidence using the GRADE methodology. Meta-analyses were performed using fixed-effect models for most outcomes and random-effects models for hematological outcomes, with adjustments for cluster RCTs. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on baseline anemia prevalence, age, and the availability of malaria prevention or management services. A total of 35 trials, involving 31,955 children, met the inclusion criteria. The findings indicated that iron supplementation does not lead to an increased risk of clinical malaria (risk ratio [RR] 0.93, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87 to 1.00; 14 trials, 7,168 children; high-quality evidence). This was true for both populations with high and low prevalence of anemia. In areas with effective malaria prevention and management services, iron (with or without folic acid) may reduce the incidence of clinical malaria (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.84 to 0.97; seven trials, 5,586 participants; low-quality evidence). However, in areas without such services, iron supplementation may slightly increase the risk of malaria (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.31; nine trials, 19,086 participants; low-quality evidence), although the lower confidence intervals suggest no significant difference. Iron supplementation did not increase the risk of severe malaria (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.98; six trials, 3,421 children; high-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in all-cause mortality between groups (control event rate 1%; low-quality evidence). When iron was combined with antimalarial treatment, it significantly reduced the incidence of clinical malaria (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.67; three trials, 728 children; high-quality evidence). Additionally, iron supplementation resulted in fewer cases of anemia at follow-up, and the average increase in hemoglobin levels from baseline was higher in children receiving iron. In conclusion, iron supplementation does not increase the risk of clinical malaria when adequate malaria prevention or management services are in place. In resource-limited settings, iron can be safely administered without prior screening for anemia or iron deficiency, provided that effective malaria prevention or management measures are implemented.
